gloss.intro: The words developers (and the AI teams) use, in plain English.
gloss.switch: 📖 Make plain the jargon of the trade
gloss.switch.help: Words with a dotted underline get a plain explanation when thou hoverest over them.
gloss.backlog.text: The waiting list of ideas and work not yet planned in, with the most important at the top. Nothing there is worked upon till it moveth to To be done.
gloss.sprint.text: A short, fixed stretch of work (often one or two weeks, never more than a month) with a goal and an agreed set of cards to finish.
gloss.standup.text: A quick daily check-in: what each team member did, what he doth next, and what stayeth him. In Scrum it is called the daily scrum.
gloss.bug.text: Something that worketh not as it should.
gloss.test.text: A check that something worketh the way it should. Some tests the computer runneth of itself every time the code changeth; others are thee trying a finished card ere thou accept it.
gloss.commit.text: A saved snapshot of the code, with a short note of what changed. Thou canst ever return to one.
gloss.push.text: Sending thy saved snapshots (commits) from this computer to the shared copy online, such as GitHub, so they be backed up and others may get them.
gloss.branch.text: A separate line of work in the code, so changes may be made without touching the main version.
gloss.merge.text: Joining the changes from one branch into another, usually back into the main version.
gloss.repo.text: The project's folder of code with its full history of commits. It may live on thy computer, on GitHub, or both.
gloss.refactor.text: Tidying the code without changing what it doth: smaller files, clearer names, less repetition.
gloss.deploy.text: Copying a new version of the software onto the computers that run it, such as a test copy or the live service.
gloss.kanban.text: A way of working where cards move across a board's columns (like To do, In progress, Done) and the team limiteth how much is in progress at once, so work keepeth flowing.
gloss.wip.text: WIP is short for work in progress. A WIP limit is the most cards a column should hold at once, so the team finisheth things ere it start more.
gloss.pr.text: Asking for a branch's changes to be checked and merged into the main version. Some sites call it a merge request.
gloss.hook.text: A small command that runneth of itself at a set moment, for example when an AI session startheth, so the team heareth thy comments.
gloss.token.text: The small pieces of text an AI readeth and writeth, about three quarters of a word each. AI use is counted in tokens, so fewer tokens leave more of thy plan.
gloss.agent.text: An AI that worketh on a task by itself: readeth the code, maketh changes, runneth checks and reporteth back. Its work still getteth checked.

gloss.title: 📖 Words made plain
gloss.about: Free training in plain language: every word thou meetest from a first idea to a service people rely upon, with Agile, building, keeping it safe and working with AI along the way.
gloss.about.noai: Free training in plain language: every word thou meetest from a first idea to a service people rely upon, with Agile, building and keeping it safe along the way.
gloss.g.team: 🤝 Working as a team (and with AI)
gloss.card.text: One piece of work: a task, a bug or an idea. It moveth across the columns till it be done.
gloss.project.text: A board for one thing thou wouldst have done, such as an app, a garden shed or a journey. It holdeth the cards.
gloss.forteam.text: The column for cards that are the company's turn again, for example after thou hast answered its question or asked for a change.
gloss.lead.text: The AI helper in charge of a project. It taketh up thy cards, shareth out the work, and asketh thee when it hath need of thee.
gloss.agentprog.text: The AI program upon thy computer, such as Claude Code, that the board startheth when there is work for thy helpers.
gloss.dispatcher.text: The part of the board that readeth a new card or comment and decideth who taketh it up. Simple rules first, a small AI only when it is unsure.
gloss.space.text: A company of projects that belong together, like a folder for boards. 🪐 marketh one.
gloss.playground.text: A ready-made project for a friend to try AI-gile in, with an invite code to send him.
gloss.hyperfocus.text: 🎯 Showeth only one project and thy messages, so that nothing else plucketh at thee. The teams carry on as ever.
gloss.qa.text: Short for quality assurance: all that is done to make sure work is right ere it goeth live. In AI-gile that meaneth the automatic checks: when QA is red, something failed, and it cannot go live till that be mended.
gloss.release.text: A named bundle of finished work that goeth live together, with short notes of what hath changed. 🚀 Releases writeth the notes from the cards that are done.
gloss.rollback.text: Going back to the last version that worked when a new one causeth trouble. In AI-gile, Roll back gathereth the undo steps written on each change into one checklist.
gloss.live.text: The true version that folk do use, as against a copy for trying things. Developers call it also production.
gloss.change.text: A planned change to aught that folk rely upon, written down first: what, wherefore, the risk, when, and how to undo it. Begin one with 🔀 Raise a change.
gloss.risk.text: Something that might go amiss, scored by how likely and how grievous it would be. ⚠️ Risks keepeth them in one list, highest score first, each with a day to look again.
gloss.chgwin.text: The hours when changes may go live, such as a quiet Tuesday evening. Outside a window a change card may not be finished, unless it be an emergency.
gloss.gonogo.text: A last check just ere a change goeth live: each person who must approve saith Go or No go. It goeth ahead only when all say Go.
gloss.approval.text: Awaiting a yea ere work beginneth. A card a friend raiseth, or a change, waiteth in ✅ Approvals till thou approvest or declinest it.
gloss.quiettime.text: A stretch of time, like during a live stream, a demo or overnight, when nothing goeth live. The teams keep working and testing, but going live waiteth till it endeth. Elsewhere it is called a change freeze.
gloss.service.text: Something thou hast built that folk rely upon, as a website or an app, tended so it keepeth working. Tick “This project is a service” and say what it offereth, who useth it and who is on call.
gloss.uptime.text: A check that runneth of itself every few minutes, to see thy service yet answereth. If it faileth several times together, AI-gile openeth an incident card of its own accord.
gloss.statuspage.text: A public page that showeth whether a service worketh (green, orange or red) with the latest tidings, so they that use it may look instead of asking.
gloss.incident.text: Something that is broken or not working properly for those using it right now, like the website being down or very slow. A 🔥 incident card leapeth the queue: getting it working again cometh first.
gloss.major.text: A great incident: many folk afflicted, or coin or data in peril. One button setteth every team upon it (swarm), rouseth whoever is on call and asketh a status line every thirty minutes.
gloss.oncall.text: Being the one who answereth when aught breaketh, even by night. Each service hath an on-call team member who is roused first for its incidents.
gloss.replyby.also: times of answer,reply-by time,reply-by times,response target
gloss.replyby.text: How long a card may wait for a first answer, as an hour for an incident. Thereafter it beareth a red clock, so naught is quietly forgot. Called also a response target.
gloss.postmortem.text: A short look back after an incident: what befell, what helped and what to change, blaming no one. An incident may not be closed without one.
gloss.problem.text: The hidden cause behind one incident or more. A 🧩 problem card gathereth incidents that keep returning, so the cause be found and mended for good.
gloss.rootcause.text: The true reason a thing broke, not merely what thou sawest go amiss. Mend the root cause and the incident returneth no more.
gloss.workaround.text: A way to keep things working till the true mending be ready, as restarting a thing when it sticketh. 'Tis written upon the problem card, so none need puzzle it out again.
gloss.knownerror.text: A problem whose cause is understood but is not yet mended, usually with a workaround written down. 🧩 Known errors listeth them, so all use the workaround instead of digging again.
gloss.runbook.text: Instructions step by step for mending a known kind of trouble, that it be done the same way, swiftly, every time. After a grave mischance the team may propose one for thee to OK.
gloss.backup.text: A saved copy of thy data from before, to fall back upon if aught be lost or marred. AI-gile maketh a backup of thy boards every day.
gloss.restore.text: Putting data back from a backup. A backup truly counteth only once thou knowest it can be restored, so 'tis worth the trying now and then.
gloss.dod.text: The team’s short checklist of what “finished” meaneth, as tested and explained, ere a card be handed thee. Its twin, the Definition of Ready, saith when a card is clear enough to begin.
gloss.testpile.text: The finished cards awaiting thy trial, one after another. Accept one or send it back with a note, and the next cometh up.
gloss.retro.text: A regular look back at how the team worketh, to agree on one or two things to do better the next time. Short for retrospective. In AI-gile a retro suggesteth a change to the team's ways of working, and thou sayest Go or Not yet.
gloss.peerreview.text: A second pair of eyes: someone other than the author checketh the work ere it reacheth thee, so fewer mistakes pass through. In AI-gile another AI checketh each card.
gloss.swarm.text: All hands on deck: many people drop other work to mend one urgent thing together till it be sorted. In AI-gile every team helpeth on one project, and other projects wait meanwhile.
gloss.scrummaster.text: In Scrum, the person who helpeth the team work well: clearing what blocketh them, keeping meetings on track and coaching good habits, without bossing any. In AI-gile the Lead Scrum Master spieth stuck cards, nudgeth the teams and remindeth thee of what is waiting, across every project.
gloss.scrummaster.text.noai: In Scrum, the person who helpeth the team work well: clearing what blocketh them, keeping meetings on track and coaching good habits, without bossing any. Without AI, AI-gile's version spieth stuck cards and worketh with fixed commands, like sorting To be done.
gloss.discovery.text: The early stage of finding out which problem is worth the solving, and for whom, ere anything be built.
gloss.problemstmt.text: One or two sentences saying who hath a trouble, what it is and why it mattereth, so that all take aim at the same mark.
gloss.user.text: A person who useth what thou buildest. His needs are what the work is for.
gloss.stakeholder.text: Any who careth how the work turneth out or is touched by it, like those who pay for it, use it or uphold it.
gloss.persona.text: A made-up but lifelike person who standeth for one kind of user, so the team may ask "would Sam find this easy?"
gloss.userresearch.text: Speaking with and watching real people to learn what they need, rather than guessing.
gloss.journey.text: The steps a person taketh to get a thing done, from first hearing of it to the finishing, also beyond thy product. Drawing it out showeth where they stick.
gloss.painpoint.text: Something that vexeth or hindereth people today. Good products take pain points away.
gloss.assumption.text: Something thou believest but hast not yet checked. Writing assumptions down showeth what to test first.
gloss.hypothesis.text: A best guess thou meanest to check, with what thou lookest to happen, like "people will sign up if the first month be free".
gloss.experiment.text: A small planned trial to learn whether an idea worketh, ere thou stake much upon it.
gloss.poc.text: A quick rough try to see whether an idea can work at all. It is usually cast aside once thou hast the answer.
gloss.prototype.text: An early model of the product, often pictures to click upon, to try the idea on people ere it be built aright.
gloss.wireframe.text: A simple sketch of a screen showing where things go, without colours or true content.
gloss.mockup.text: A detailed picture of how a screen shall look, with true colours and text, but nothing yet worketh.
gloss.bizcase.text: The reasons for doing a project: what it costeth, what it bringeth in or saveth, and the risks.
gloss.feasibility.text: Whether a thing can truly be built and kept with the time, coin and skills thou hast.
gloss.outcome.text: The change thou wouldst have for people, like fewer missed appointments. It mattereth more than how much thou buildest.
gloss.output.text: Something the team maketh, like a new screen or a report. The making of it helpeth no one of itself.
gloss.successmetric.text: A number that telleth thee whether the work did what it was for, like more people finishing their order.
gloss.kpi.text: An important number thou watchest to see whether all goeth well, like sign-ups per week.
gloss.okr.text: A way of setting goals: the objective saith what thou wouldst have, and a few key results are the numbers that show thou hast come there.
gloss.product.text: The thing being built and kept for its users, such as an app, a website or a tool.
gloss.vision.text: A short statement of whom the product helpeth and whither it heads in the long run.
gloss.po.text: The person who decideth what is built and in what order, so the team ever worketh on what mattereth most. In AI-gile that is thee.
gloss.pm.text: The person who looketh to a product's direction: which troubles it solveth, for whom and why. PM may also mean project manager, so check which.
gloss.projmgr.text: The person who keepeth a project on time and within the purse, marking who doth what and by when.
gloss.roadmap.text: A rough plan of what cometh over the next months, in order. It showeth the road, not exact dates, and changeth as thou learnest.
gloss.milestone.text: A point in a project worth the marking, like "first version live" or "100 users".
gloss.mvp.text: The smallest version of a product that is yet useful to real people, so thou mayest learn from them betimes.
gloss.requirement.text: Something the finished product must do or be.
gloss.scope.text: What is included in the work and, no less important, what is not.
gloss.scopecreep.text: When more and more is added to the work bit by bit, with none agreeing the extra time or cost, so that it never quite endeth.
gloss.feature.text: One thing the product can do for people, like "reset thy password".
gloss.epic.text: A great piece of work, too large for one go, so it is split into smaller cards.
gloss.story.text: A small piece of work written from the user's side: "As a shopper, I want to save my basket, so I may finish later." It beginneth a conversation about what to build.
gloss.ac.text: The checks one card must pass to count as done, agreed ere work beginneth, like "the basket is still there after I log out and in again".
gloss.task.text: A single job to be done, often one small step of a greater story.
gloss.ticket.text: Another word for a card: one piece of work or one request, tracked from start to finish.
gloss.priority.text: How important or urgent a thing is against all the rest, so the most important work goeth first.
gloss.prioritise.text: Putting work in order of importance. A common way is MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.
gloss.estimate.text: A best guess at how great or how long a piece of work is. It is a guess, not a promise.
gloss.storypoints.text: A way of guessing the size of work by comparing cards one with another ("about twice as large as that one") rather than in hours. They are not for comparing teams.
gloss.tshirt.text: Guessing the size of work as S, M, L or XL. Quick, and good enough for early planning.
gloss.poker.text: A game for estimating: all show a size card at the same moment, then the highest and lowest tell why.
gloss.dependency.text: When one piece of work cannot start or finish until another doth.
gloss.blocker.text: Anything staying work from moving forward this moment, like a missing answer or a broken tool.
gloss.deadline.text: The date by which a thing must be finished.
gloss.deliverable.text: Something solid the work yieldeth and handeth over, like a working page or a report.
gloss.forecast.text: A prophecy of what is likely to happen, like when the work shall be done, based on what thou knowest so far.
gloss.metric.text: Anything thou measurest and trackest over time, like page visits or how long a fix taketh.
gloss.feedback.text: What people tell thee of thy work, good and ill. To have it early and often is the heart of Agile.
gloss.agile.text: A way of working in small steps: build a little, show real results often, learn from what people say and change the plan as thou goest, rather than planning all up front.
gloss.manifesto.text: A short statement written in 2001 by makers of software. It setteth people, working results, close work with customers and answering to change above heavy plans and paperwork.
gloss.waterfall.text: The older way of working: plan all, then build it all, then test it all, one stage after another. Changes late on are hard and costly.
gloss.iteration.text: One round of building something, checking it and mending it. Agile work is a chain of these, and a sprint is one kind.
gloss.increment.text: A new working piece added to the product in a sprint or round of work, which fitteth with what was there before.
gloss.scrum.text: A popular Agile way of working: a small team worketh in short sprints toward a goal, with set roles and a few regular meetings to plan, check and mend.
gloss.scrumteam.text: The small company that doth the work in Scrum: a product owner, a Scrum Master and the developers.
gloss.ceremonies.text: The regular meetings in Scrum: sprint planning, the daily scrum, the sprint review and the retro. Many call them ceremonies.
gloss.sprintplan.text: The meeting at the start of a sprint where the team agreeth why the sprint mattereth, which cards to take on and how to begin.
gloss.sprintgoal.text: One sentence saying what a sprint is for. Small tasks may change by the way, so long as the goal be met.
gloss.sprintbacklog.text: The cards picked for the present sprint, with the team's plan for doing them.
gloss.productbacklog.text: The whole ordered list of all that might be built for the product, the most important at the top. It keepeth changing as thou learnest.
gloss.productgoal.text: The greater result the product worketh toward, which helpeth the team choose what to do next.
gloss.refinement.text: Going through the backlog at regular times to tidy, split, order and add detail to cards, so they be ready to take up. Also called backlog grooming.
gloss.sprintreview.text: A meeting at the end of a sprint where the team showeth what it finished and heareth what people think, to decide what cometh next.
gloss.demo.text: Showing finished work working, live, to those who asked for it.
gloss.timebox.text: A fixed measure of time for something. When it runneth out thou stoppest, even if not all be done.
gloss.velocity.text: How much work a team usually finisheth in a sprint, used to plan how much to take on the next time. It is no score of how hard folk labour.
gloss.capacity.text: How much work the team can take on in a season, after holidays and other tasks.
gloss.burndown.text: A chart of the work left in a sprint falling day by day. If the line lieth flat, something is stuck.
gloss.burnup.text: A chart of finished work rising over time, beside the total planned, so thou mayest see when thou shalt arrive.
gloss.kanbanboard.text: The board itself: a column for each stage of the work, with cards moving across.
gloss.pullsys.text: A way of working where new work beginneth only when someone hath room to take it on, rather than being pushed upon a full plate.
gloss.flow.text: How smoothly work moveth across the board. Good flow meaneth cards keep moving rather than piling up.
gloss.leadtime.text: How long it taketh from someone asking for a thing to its being finished.
gloss.cycletime.text: How long a card taketh from when work truly beginneth upon it to when it is finished.
gloss.throughput.text: How many cards get finished in a week, or in any set time.
gloss.bottleneck.text: The one stage where work pileth up and hindereth all behind it, like the narrow neck of a bottle.
gloss.swimlane.text: A row across the board that gathereth cards of one kind, such as urgent work or one team's cards.
gloss.lean.text: A way of working that cutteth out waste (anything that helpeth not the customer) and keepeth work flowing.
gloss.waste.text: In Lean, anything that taketh effort but helpeth not the customer, like waiting, rework or building things none useth.
gloss.kaizen.text: Getting a little better all the time through small regular changes, then checking they helped. Retros are one way to do it. Also called kaizen.
gloss.selforg.text: A team that decideth for itself how to do the work, rather than being told step by step.
gloss.crossfunc.text: A team that hath all the skills it needeth to finish the work itself, like design, building and testing.
gloss.spike.text: A short, timeboxed bit of research to answer a question ere thou commit to the true work.
gloss.rework.text: Doing work again because it was not right the first time.
gloss.safe.text: Ways of using Agile across many teams in a great organisation. SAFe (the Scaled Agile Framework) is one well known example.
gloss.code.text: The written instructions that tell a computer what to do. Also called source code.
gloss.proglang.text: A tongue for writing code, such as JavaScript, Python or Java. Different ones suit different tasks.
gloss.developer.text: Someone who writeth and changeth code. Also called a programmer or software engineer.
gloss.software.text: Programs that run on computers and phones, as opposed to the machines themselves (the hardware).
gloss.app.text: Short for application: a program people use to get a thing done, on a phone, a computer or in a web browser.
gloss.webapp.text: An app that runneth in a web browser, so there is nothing to install.
gloss.frontend.text: The part of an app thou seest and clickest upon: the screens, buttons and words, often in thy browser.
gloss.backend.text: The behind-the-scenes part of an app that keepeth the data and doth the work when thou clickest something, like checking thy password.
gloss.fullstack.text: Working upon both the front end and the back end.
gloss.ui.text: What a person seeth and useth on screen: layout, buttons, menus and text.
gloss.ux.text: How it feeleth to use something: easy, clear and pleasant, or confusing and slow.
gloss.accessibility.text: Making things usable by all, including people who cannot see well, cannot use a mouse or use a screen reader.
gloss.responsive.text: Making pages fit and work well on any screen size, from a phone to a great monitor.
gloss.designsys.text: A shared kit of colours, fonts, buttons and rules, so every screen looketh and behaveth the same way.
gloss.architecture.text: The whole shape of a system: what the main parts are and how they speak one with another.
gloss.database.text: An orderly store of information, like a very mighty spreadsheet that the app can read and change.
gloss.schema.text: The layout of a database: which tables of information it hath and what goeth in each.
gloss.sql.text: Short for structured query language: the tongue used to ask many databases for information or to change it.
gloss.data.text: Information kept by a computer, like names, orders or settings.
gloss.server.text: A computer that is ever on and answereth requests from other computers, like sending a web page when thou visitest it.
gloss.client.text: The side that asketh for something, usually thy browser or app, speaking to a server. In business it also meaneth just a customer.
gloss.api.text: Short for application programming interface: a set menu of requests one program may make of another, like asking a weather service for today's forecast.
gloss.endpoint.text: One item on an API's menu: a web address a program can call to get or send something.
gloss.integration.text: Joining two systems so they work together, like thy shop sending orders to thy accounts software.
gloss.webhook.text: A message one system sendeth to another of itself the moment something happeneth, like "payment received".
gloss.library.text: Ready-made code someone else wrote that thou mayest reuse instead of writing it thyself.
gloss.framework.text: A ready-made structure for building an app that decideth much of how the code is laid out, like a house frame thou fillest in.
gloss.sdk.text: A box of tools, code and examples for building software for one platform or service.
gloss.softdep.text: A library or tool thy code needeth to work. Keeping them up to date mattereth for safety.
gloss.package.text: A bundle of ready-made code thou canst install and use in a project.
gloss.pkgmgr.text: A tool that fetcheth and updateth the packages thy code dependeth on. npm is a common one.
gloss.git.text: The most widely used tool for keeping the history of code changes, as commits and branches.
gloss.github.text: A website that keepeth Git repos online, so teams may share code, review changes and track work.
gloss.vcs.text: Keeping a full history of every change to the files, so thou mayest see who changed what and go back if need be. Git doth this.
gloss.clone.text: Making thine own full copy of a repo, with its history, upon thy computer.
gloss.pull.text: Fetching the latest commits from the shared copy (like GitHub) onto thy computer. The opposite of push.
gloss.mainbranch.text: The official version of the code that all work from, often called main or master.
gloss.conflict.text: When two changes touch the same lines in different ways, so the computer cannot join them and a person must choose.
gloss.diff.text: A view showing exactly what changed between two versions: lines added and lines taken away.
gloss.fork.text: Thine own copy of another's repo, which thou mayest change without touching his.
gloss.script.text: A short program that doth one task of itself, like tidying files or starting the app.
gloss.build.text: Turning the code into something ready to run, or the ready-to-run result itself.
gloss.compile.text: Translating code that people wrote into a form the computer can run directly.
gloss.cli.text: A text window where thou typest instructions for the computer instead of clicking. Also called the terminal.
gloss.config.text: The settings that rule how software behaveth, kept apart from the code so they be easy to change.
gloss.envvar.text: A setting handed to a program when it startheth, often used for addresses or passwords so they be not written into the code.
gloss.debugging.text: Hunting down why something worketh not, and mending it.
gloss.pairing.text: Two people (or a person and an AI) working on the same code together, one typing and one checking.
gloss.docs.text: Written explanations of how something worketh or how to use it.
gloss.readme.text: The first file to read in a repo: what the project is and how to get it running.
gloss.legacy.text: An older system still in use that is hard to change, often because few yet understand it.
gloss.techdebt.text: Shortcuts that save time now but make later changes slower, like a loan that gathereth interest. Refactoring payeth it down.
gloss.autotest.text: A check the computer runneth of itself every time the code changeth, to catch mistakes betimes.
gloss.manualtest.text: A person trying the work by hand to see whether it behaveth as it should.
gloss.unittest.text: A small automatic check of one tiny piece of code upon its own.
gloss.integtest.text: A check that several parts work rightly together, not just one at a time.
gloss.endtoend.text: A test that acteth like a real user from start to finish, such as signing up, buying and paying.
gloss.uat.text: Those who asked for the work try it themselves and say whether it doth what they need. AI-gile's test pile is its version of this.
gloss.regression.text: Something that used to work but broke after a change. Regression tests check that the old things yet work.
gloss.smoke.text: A very quick check that the main things work at all, for example right after a change goeth live. If it fail, stop and look.
gloss.exploratory.text: Trying the product freely and poking at it in diverse ways, to find troubles that planned checks would miss.
gloss.testcase.text: One written scenario to try: the steps, and what should happen.
gloss.coverage.text: How much of the code is checked by automatic tests. More is usually safer, but high coverage alone proveth not that it worketh well.
gloss.testdata.text: Made-up example information used while testing, so no real person's private matters be exposed.
gloss.edgecase.text: An unusual case at the limits, like an empty form or a name with an apostrophe, where things oft break.
gloss.happypath.text: The ordinary road where all goeth right. Good testing also trieth the unhappy paths.
gloss.perftest.text: Checking how fast something is and how well it copeth under strain.
gloss.loadtest.text: Checking how a system copeth when many people use it at once.
gloss.sectest.text: Looking for weaknesses that might let someone misuse a system or see what he should not.
gloss.accesstest.text: Checking that people of different abilities can use the product, including with a screen reader or only a keyboard.
gloss.linting.text: An automatic check that spotteth likely mistakes and untidy style in code, like a spelling checker for programs.
gloss.static.text: Checking code for troubles by reading it automatically, without running it.
gloss.flaky.text: A test that sometimes passeth and sometimes faileth for no clear reason, so it cannot be fully trusted.
gloss.repro.text: Making a bug happen again on purpose by following the same steps, so it may be studied and mended. Writing those steps down is the most useful part of a bug report.
gloss.severity.text: How grave a problem's effect is, from a small vexation to everything stopping.
gloss.devops.text: A way of working where those who build software and those who run it work as one team, with much automation, so changes go live often and safely.
gloss.cicd.text: All men's changes are joined into the main version often and checked automatically each time (continuous integration), so the software is ever ready to go live at the press of a button (continuous delivery).
gloss.contdeploy.text: One step beyond continuous delivery: every change that passeth the checks goeth live of itself, with no button to press.
gloss.pipeline.text: The automatic series of steps a change goeth through on its way to live, like build, test, then deploy.
gloss.environment.text: One separate copy of the system for one purpose, such as one to build in, one to test in and the live one.
gloss.devenv.text: The copy a developer worketh in, often upon his own computer, where breaking things harmeth none.
gloss.testenv.text: A separate copy of the system used just for testing, so the real service be not touched.
gloss.staging.text: A last copy set up just like live, for a final check ere a change goeth live.
gloss.artifact.text: The file or bundle a build produceth, ready to be stored, checked or put live.
gloss.hotfix.text: An urgent fix put live quickly, outside the usual plan, because something important is broken.
gloss.patch.text: A small update that mendeth a bug or closeth a security hole. Applying security patches quickly mattereth.
gloss.version.text: A label like 2.4.1 that saith which release thou hast. Often the first number changeth for great changes and the last for small fixes.
gloss.relnotes.text: A short plain list of what changed in a release, for those who use it, including fixes and known limits. Also called a changelog.
gloss.flag.text: An on and off switch for a feature, so new work may go live hidden and be turned on (or off again) without a new release.
gloss.rollfwd.text: Mending a bad release by quickly putting out a new, corrected version instead of going back to the old one.
gloss.canary.text: Putting a change live for a small company first, and for all only once it looketh fine. Named after the canaries miners took underground as an early warning.
gloss.bluegreen.text: Keeping two copies of the live system and switching people over to the new one in one go, so thou canst switch straight back if it go ill.
gloss.zerodown.text: Putting a new version live without the service ever stopping for its users.
gloss.chgenable.text: Helping changes to succeed: weighing the risk, getting the right approval and picking a good hour. Also called change management.
gloss.cab.text: A company that looketh over important changes and agreeth whether and when they may go ahead.
gloss.stdchange.text: A low-risk change done the same tried and tested way each time, so it is approved beforehand.
gloss.normchange.text: A change that needeth to be checked and approved ere it goeth ahead.
gloss.emergchange.text: A change that must happen right away to mend or prevent grave trouble, with a quicker approval to match.
gloss.automation.text: Getting the computer to do a repeated task of itself, so it is quicker and done the same way every time.
gloss.infra.text: The machines, networks and services that software runneth upon.
gloss.iac.text: Describing thy servers and settings in files kept with the code, so they may be rebuilt exactly the same way every time.
gloss.cloud.text: Renting computers, storage and services from a great provider over the internet, instead of owning the machines thyself.
gloss.provider.text: A company that rentheth out computing over the internet, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud.
gloss.hosting.text: Where thy app or website liveth and runneth so people can reach it, usually rented from a company.
gloss.domain.text: The web address people type, like example.com. Thou rentest it by the year, so it must be renewed.
gloss.dns.text: Short for domain name system: the internet's book of addresses, which turneth a name like example.com into the address of the right computer.
gloss.container.text: A sealed package holding an app and all it needeth, so it runneth the same on any computer. Docker is the best known tool.
gloss.vm.text: A pretend computer running inside a real one, so one great machine may act as many.
gloss.serverless.text: Running code without tending any servers thyself: the provider runneth it when needed and thou payest for what thou usest.
gloss.lb.text: Something that spreadeth visitors across several servers, so that no single one be overwhelmed.
gloss.cache.text: A handy store of recent results kept close by, so the same thing need not be fetched or worked out again. Clearing it can mend pages that look out of date.
gloss.cdn.text: A worldwide set of servers holding copies of thy pages and pictures near thy visitors, so they load quickly.
gloss.migration.text: Moving data or systems from an old setup to a new one, or carefully changing how a database is laid out.
gloss.svcmgmt.text: All that is needed to keep a service useful and working for those who rely upon it, day after day.
gloss.itil.text: A widely used guide to good service management, covering things like incidents, problems and changes. The name once stood for IT Infrastructure Library.
gloss.itsm.text: Running technology as a service for people, with clear ways to handle requests, incidents, changes and improvements.
gloss.managed.text: A service that another runneth and looketh to for thee, under an agreement about how well it must work.
gloss.svcowner.text: The person who answereth for a service as a whole: how well it worketh, what it costeth and how it improveth.
gloss.sla.text: A written promise to customers of how well a service shall work, like "up 99.9% of the time" or "answered within an hour", often with coin returned if it be broken.
gloss.slo.text: The team's own target for how well a service should work over a season, usually set a little stricter than the SLA to be safe.
gloss.sli.text: The actual measurement thou checkest against a target, like the share of visits that loaded fine.
gloss.uptimepct.text: How much of the time a service is working, usually as a percentage. 99.9% yet alloweth about 43 minutes down a month.
gloss.availability.text: Whether people can use a service when they have need, often measured as uptime.
gloss.downtime.text: Time when a service worketh not or is switched off, planned or not.
gloss.errorbudget.text: The small amount of failure thy reliability target alloweth. While some is left thou mayest take risks with changes; once it is spent, thou slowest.
gloss.outage.text: A time when a service is down or badly broken for its users.
gloss.degraded.text: Working, but ill: slow, or with some parts not working.
gloss.monitoring.text: Watching a service automatically all the time, so troubles are spied, ideally ere users notice.
gloss.observability.text: How well thou canst tell what passeth within a system from the outside, using its logs, numbers and traces.
gloss.log.text: A running diary a program keepeth of what it doth, used to work out what went amiss.
gloss.trace.text: A record of how one request travelleth through the diverse parts of a system, step by step, showing where it slowed.
gloss.latency.text: How long something taketh to answer, like the wait between clicking and the page appearing.
gloss.alert.text: An automatic message that something needeth attention, like the website not answering.
gloss.alertfatigue.text: When there be so many alerts that people begin to ignore them, the important ones too.
gloss.dashboard.text: A screen showing the most important numbers and statuses at a glance.
gloss.paging.text: Urgently calling or waking the on-call person about a problem.
gloss.escalation.text: Bringing in one of more skill or authority when an issue cannot be sorted at the present level, or not fast enough.
gloss.triage.text: Quickly sorting incoming issues by how urgent and important they be, so the worst is handled first.
gloss.impact.text: How much something toucheth people: how many, and how sorely.
gloss.urgency.text: How quickly something must be dealt with. Impact and urgency together set the priority.
gloss.plevels.text: Labels for how urgent an issue is. P1 is the gravest and needeth action straightway.
gloss.queue.text: The list of requests and incidents waiting to be taken up.
gloss.tiers.text: Levels of support: first line taketh the call and mendeth simple things; second line hath deeper skills for harder ones. Also called tier 1 and tier 2.
gloss.ic.text: The one person who leadeth the response to an incident, so all know who decideth and who doth what.
gloss.responsetime.text: How long it taketh ere someone first taketh up a request or incident.
gloss.resolution.text: How long it taketh to sort out a request or incident fully, from report to mended.
gloss.mttr.text: On average, how long it taketh to get a service working again after it breaketh. MTTR can mean slightly different things, so say what thou measurest.
gloss.mtbf.text: On average, how long a service runneth before something breaketh.
gloss.cmdb.text: The list of all thy configuration items and how they connect, so thou mayest see what dependeth on what.
gloss.asset.text: Anything of value thou ownest or payest for to run the service, like a laptop, a software licence or a domain.
gloss.capplan.text: Making sure there shall be enough computer power, storage and people for what is coming.
gloss.scaling.text: Coping with more users by giving a machine more power (scaling up) or adding more machines (scaling out).
gloss.bcp.text: Plans for keeping the important things going when something great goeth wrong, like losing an office, a key supplier or the computers.
gloss.dr.text: The plan and tools for getting a service back after something grave, like losing a whole data centre.
gloss.rto.text: The longest a service may be down after a disaster ere it must be working again.
gloss.rpo.text: How much recent data thou couldst afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of one hour meaneth backups at least every hour.
gloss.redundancy.text: Having spares ready, like a second server, so one failure stoppeth not the service.
gloss.failover.text: Switching over to a spare system of itself when the usual one faileth.
gloss.spof.text: One part that bringeth all down with it when it breaketh, because there is no spare.
gloss.maintwin.text: A planned time when a service may be paused or slow for upkeep, announced to users beforehand.
gloss.handover.text: Passing work, knowledge and responsibility to another person or team, so nothing be dropped.
gloss.kb.text: A collection of help articles and answers, for users and for the team.
gloss.csat.text: A score from users saying how glad they were, often asked after a request is closed.
gloss.supplier.text: An outside company thou reliest upon, like thy hosting provider. Also called a vendor or third party.
gloss.retire.text: Switching a service off for good, safely: telling its users, dealing with its data and access, and stopping its costs.
gloss.eol.text: When a product ceaseth to get updates or support from its maker, so it should be replaced.
gloss.cybersec.text: Protecting systems and data from being broken into, stolen or damaged.
gloss.authn.text: Checking who someone is, usually with a password or a code. Often shortened to authn.
gloss.authz.text: Checking what someone is allowed to do once thou knowest who he is. Often shortened to authz.
gloss.mfa.text: Logging in with two or more proofs, like a password plus a code upon thy phone. Also called two-factor (2FA).
gloss.sso.text: Logging in once to get into many systems, like using thy work account everywhere.
gloss.pwmgr.text: An app that createth strong passwords and remembereth them for thee.
gloss.secret.text: A password, key or other private code a program useth to get into something. It must never be shared or written into the code.
gloss.apikey.text: A secret code that letteth a program use another service's API, and showeth who useth (and payeth for) it.
gloss.accesstoken.text: A temporary pass that proveth a program is allowed in, so it needeth not thy password each time. Not the same as an AI token.
gloss.encryption.text: Scrambling information so that only one with the right key can read it.
gloss.https.text: The secure way web pages travel, shown by the padlock in thy browser, so that none in between can read or change them.
gloss.cert.text: A digital ID card that letteth a website prove who it is and use HTTPS. It expireth, so it must be renewed.
gloss.permissions.text: The rules for who may see or change what.
gloss.leastpriv.text: Giving each person or program only the access he truly needeth, for only as long as he needeth it.
gloss.rbac.text: Giving access by role, like viewer or editor, rather than person by person.
gloss.vuln.text: A weakness that someone could use to break in or cause harm.
gloss.zeroday.text: A weakness attackers know of ere the makers have had any time to mend it.
gloss.malware.text: Harmful software, like viruses, made to damage, spy or steal.
gloss.ransomware.text: Malware that locketh up thy files and demandeth coin to unlock them. Good backups are the best defence.
gloss.phishing.text: False messages that try to trick thee into giving away passwords or coin, or opening something harmful.
gloss.socialeng.text: Tricking people, rather than computers, into giving access, like a false call from "IT support".
gloss.firewall.text: A guard that decideth which network traffic may come in or go out.
gloss.vpn.text: Short for virtual private network: a private, scrambled link over the internet, often used to reach work systems safely.
gloss.ddos.text: Flooding a service with so much false traffic that real people cannot use it. DDoS meaneth it cometh from many computers at once.
gloss.pentest.text: Hiring friendly experts to try to break in, so weaknesses are found ere real attackers find them.
gloss.audit.text: A careful check of how well something is protected, against a list of good practice.
gloss.threatmodel.text: Thinking through who might attack something, how, and what thou wouldst do to stop them.
gloss.breach.text: When private information getteth out to those who should not have it, or is lost or changed without leave.
gloss.pii.text: Any information about a person who can be identified, like a name, email address or place. Also called PII.
gloss.gdpr.text: The European law on personal data (the UK hath its own version): gather only what thou needest, keep it safe, and let people see or delete theirs.
gloss.dataprot.text: Looking after personal data properly and within the law.
gloss.privacypolicy.text: A public page saying what personal data thou gatherest, why, and what thou doest with it.
gloss.consent.text: A person's clear, free yes to his data being used in a particular way. He may take it back at any time.
gloss.cookie.text: A small file a website saveth in thy browser to remember things, like being logged in. Some need thy consent first.
gloss.minimisation.text: Gathering and keeping only the personal data thou truly needest for the task.
gloss.retention.text: How long data is kept ere it be deleted. Keeping it no longer than needed is safer and often the law.
gloss.anon.text: Changing data so that none can reasonably be identified from it any more.
gloss.pseudo.text: Swapping names and other details for codes, with a key kept apart to link them back. It is still personal data.
gloss.dpa.text: A contract saying how a supplier may handle personal data on thy behalf.
gloss.dpia.text: A careful look, ere thou begin, at how a plan to use personal data could touch people and how to lower the risks.
gloss.auditlog.text: A record of who did what and when, so actions may be checked hereafter.
gloss.compliance.text: Following the laws, rules and standards that apply to thee, and being able to show that thou doest.
gloss.iso.text: A well known international standard for managing information security. Companies may be certified against it.
gloss.soc.text: A US report, checked by outside auditors, showing that a company looketh to customer data properly.
gloss.ai.text: Computer systems that do things we usually think need a person, like writing, answering questions or recognising pictures.
gloss.ml.text: A way of making computers learn patterns from many examples, instead of giving them exact rules.
gloss.model.text: The trained "brain" of an AI system, built by learning from vast numbers of examples. Models differ in skill, speed and price.
gloss.llm.text: An AI model trained on vast amounts of text, so that it can read and write language.
gloss.genai.text: AI that createth new things, like text, pictures or code, rather than only sorting or spotting them.
gloss.chatbot.text: A program thou speakest with in everyday language, by typing or speaking.
gloss.prompt.text: What thou givest an AI: thy question or instructions, plus anything thou handest it. Clearer prompts usually get better answers.
gloss.prompteng.text: The skill of writing prompts that get reliable, useful results.
gloss.sysprompt.text: Background instructions an AI getteth ere the conversation beginneth, setting its role and rules. They weigh more than what thou typest.
gloss.context.text: All that the AI can see while it worketh: the instructions, thy messages, files it hath read and earlier replies.
gloss.ctxwin.text: How much an AI can keep in mind at once, measured in tokens. Past that, older parts get dropped or summarised.
gloss.session.text: One working conversation with an AI, from start to finish. A new session beginneth with a fresh memory.
gloss.memory.text: Notes an AI keepeth between sessions, so it remembereth thy preferences and past decisions.
gloss.hallucination.text: When an AI saith something that soundeth sure of itself but is made up or wrong. Check important facts.
gloss.training.text: Teaching a model by showing it vast numbers of examples, ere any use it.
gloss.trainingdata.text: The examples a model learned from. Its knowledge stoppeth at the date that data was gathered.
gloss.cutoff.text: The date an AI's built-in knowledge endeth. It knoweth not of later things unless it looketh them up.
gloss.finetune.text: Extra training of an existing model on thine own examples, to make it better at one particular task.
gloss.inference.text: An AI model actually being used to answer something, as opposed to being trained.
gloss.tooluse.text: An AI being able to do things, not just talk: run commands, read files or search the web, through tools the app giveth it.
gloss.subagent.text: A helper AI to whom a main AI handeth a smaller task, and getteth the result back.
gloss.multiagent.text: Several AIs working together on one piece of work, each with its own part, like a small team.
gloss.autonomy.text: How much an AI may do on its own ere it must ask a person.
gloss.hitl.text: Keeping a person involved to check or approve what the AI doth at key points. In AI-gile that is thee.
gloss.guardrails.text: Limits and checks that keep an AI's actions safe, like needing approval ere anything goeth live. They lower the risk of mistakes, but rule them not out.
gloss.rag.text: Letting an AI look things up in thine own documents ere it answereth, so its answers rest on thy facts.
gloss.embedding.text: Turning text into a list of numbers that catcheth its meaning, so a computer may find things that mean the like.
gloss.vectordb.text: A database built to search those lists of numbers (embeddings), to find matter of a like meaning.
gloss.mcp.text: A common way to plug tools and data sources into AI apps, so that an AI may use them.
gloss.temperature.text: A setting for how adventurous an AI's answers be. Low giveth steadier, more foreseeable answers; high giveth more varied ones. Neither maketh it always right.
gloss.multimodal.text: Able to work with more than one kind of information, such as text, pictures and sound.
gloss.evals.text: A planned test of how well an AI doth on chosen examples, so thou canst compare models or prompts.
gloss.bias.text: When an AI (or a person) leaneth unfairly one way, often because of what it learned from.
gloss.responsible.text: Using AI fairly, safely and honestly, with people still answerable for the results.
gloss.injection.text: A trick where hidden instructions in a web page or file try to make an AI do something its user did not ask for.
gloss.ratelimit.text: A cap on how many requests thou mayest send to a service in a set time. Go over it and thou must wait.
gloss.usagelimit.text: How much AI work thy plan alloweth in a season, after which it pauseth or costeth more.
gloss.vibe.text: Building software mostly by describing what thou wouldst have to an AI and letting it write the code.
gloss.budget.text: The sum of coin set aside for something.
gloss.costest.text: A best guess at what something shall cost ere thou begin.
gloss.roi.text: What thou gettest back compared with what thou puttest in. If it be positive, it was worth it.
gloss.tco.text: All that something truly costeth over its whole life, not just the price to buy it: running, support, upgrades and at last retiring it.
gloss.capex.text: CapEx is coin spent up front on things thou keepest; OpEx is ongoing spending, like monthly bills.
gloss.subscription.text: Paying regularly, usually monthly or yearly, to keep using something.
gloss.saas.text: Software thou usest online and payest for by subscription, while the maker runneth it for thee.
gloss.payg.text: Paying only for what thou usest, like cloud computing or AI tokens.
gloss.overage.text: Use above what thy plan includeth, which can cost extra.
gloss.billingalert.text: A message when spending or use reacheth a level thou hast chosen. It warneth thee, but stoppeth not always further charges.
gloss.freetier.text: A free level of a paid service, with limits. Handy for starting out.
gloss.pricing.text: The diverse packages a service selleth, each with its own price and limits.
gloss.licence.text: The rules for how thou mayest use, copy, change or share something another made, such as software, fonts or pictures.
gloss.opensource.text: Software whose code any may read, use and often change for free, under the rules of its licence.
gloss.osslicence.text: The rules that come with open source code. Some let thee do almost anything (like MIT); some ask thee to share thy changes too (like GPL).
gloss.proprietary.text: Owned by a company and not free to copy or change. The opposite of open source.
gloss.copyright.text: The legal right of a creator to rule over copies of his work, including code and writing.
gloss.ip.text: Ideas and creations the law treateth as owned, like code, designs, names and logos.
gloss.tos.text: The rules thou agreest to when thou usest a service.
gloss.contract.text: A written agreement between two sides that the law shall back up.
gloss.sow.text: A document setting out exactly what work shall be done, by when and for how much.
gloss.fixedprice.text: An agreed price for the whole task, however long it taketh.
gloss.tm.text: Paying for the hours truly worked and the things truly used, rather than a set price.
gloss.invoice.text: A bill asking for payment for work done or goods supplied.
gloss.lockin.text: When moving away from a supplier is so hard or costly that thou art stuck with him.
gloss.procurement.text: The process of choosing and buying from suppliers.
gloss.servicecredit.text: Coin back or a discount thou gettest when a supplier misseth its SLA.

gloss.expiry.text: The date something ceaseth to work unless it be renewed, like a website's security certificate or its web address. AI-gile watcheth these dates and maketh one card to renew each one 30 days before, so nothing stoppeth by surprise.
gloss.desk.text: Whither come the questions and reports of those that use thy service. AI-gile sorteth each into a request, an incident or a notion, and saith so when it seemeth a thing already reported.

guide.inc.hi:
- An **incident** 🔥 is a card for "'tis broken now". It leapeth the queue and hath a red edge.
- Closing it asketh three short questions: what befell, why, what we shall change.
- If the same thing break again, gather the incidents under one **problem** 🧩 with its root cause and a workaround.
- The true mending goeth through a change request.
guide.inc.steps:
1. Raise the incident: **New card**, of the kind **🔥 incident**.
2. Mend it first. Use the workaround if the problem card hath one.
3. Move it to Done. Fill in **What befell**, **Why**, **What we shall change**, then **Done**.
4. Hath it befallen before? Bid thy chief gather the incidents under a **🧩 problem** card (the commands lie under *For the agents*).
5. The problem card showeth the **Root cause**, the **Workaround**, the incidents and the change request.
6. Later incidents join the same problem; the card listeth them all.
7. Raise a change request for the mending. The problem stayeth open till that change be done.
guide.inc.full:
- **Why it mattereth:** an incident is about returning swiftly to the wonted state. A problem is about the cause. Confound the two and thou shalt quench the selfsame fire again and again.
- **Incident:** the post-mortem layeth no blame. It saith what befell, why, and what changeth that it come not again. A risk from the register of risks that cometh to pass fileth an incident for thee.
- **Problem:** one cause, many incidents. The root cause is the reason behind the reason (not "the server was down" but "the deploy script skippeth the tests"). The workaround is what any may do till the mending ship.
- **Linking:** an incident belongeth to one problem. The link showeth upon both cards. Linking it to another problem removeth it thither.
- **Change request:** the mending is a change like any other, with a reason, a risk and a way back. The problem stayeth open till that change be done.
- **Good habits:** look upon open problems at each retro; if three incidents share a cause, make the problem; keep workarounds short enough to follow though sore pressed.
guide.inc.agents:
- Raise an incident: `aigile add <proj> "Site is down" --type incident`
- Make a problem: `aigile problem <proj> add "Deploys break the site" --incidents AIG-1,AIG-2`
- Cause and workaround: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --cause "..." --workaround "..."`
- Link a later incident: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 link AIG-12`
- Link the change request: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --change AIG-20`
guide.svc.hi:
- Tell the board which projects be **services**: what they offer, who useth them and their web address. The board then keepeth watch upon the address for thee.
- When a service ceaseth to answer, the board raiseth **one incident** of itself. A card that waiteth too long showeth a red ⏰ "reply by" clock.
- A truly dire incident hath the **🚨 Grave** button: one click rouseth the right agent and telleth thee. A public status page showeth thy friends how matters stand.
- What thou learnest is kept: **🧩 Known follies**, **📖 Runbooks** (how to mend X) and a **📝 Review after the mischance** upon each grave mischance.
- Keep an eye upon the **🗂️ Items** thy service standeth on (expiry dates, backups), the **🔐 Review of access** every 90 days, **🚀 Releases**, the **📈 Betterments** list and, once a month, the **📆 Review** (with a monthly token cap, if thou wilt).
guide.svc.steps:
1. Upon the project board click **🎨 Look**. In **The settings of the project** find the **🛎️ Service** part. Tick **This project is a service** and fill in what it offereth, who useth it and its web address.
2. Choose the **On-call agent** (the chief, by default) and tick **Public** if friends may see it upon the status page. If thou wilt, type a **Monthly token cap**, that one project devour not the whole purse. Click **Keep**.
3. Look upon the project's dot at **Home**: green signifieth the address answereth. If it cease to answer, an incident card appeareth of itself.
4. Open that incident card. A dire one? Click **🚨 Grave**. Click **End the grave mischance** when it is past.
5. Cards that wait too long show a red ⏰. Open those first. The inbox filter **Desk: mischances** showeth only incidents from friends and the feedback form.
6. Click **⋯ More** upon the board, then **🗂️ Items**. Click **+ Add an item** for each server, domain, certificate, key, repo or purveyor. Add an expiry date and, for data, where 'tis backed up and how oft. Click **Backed up this day** after each backup.
7. Upon an incident card, look to the **📖 Runbooks** box: it listeth the how-to notes that match. Click **Open** to read one.
8. When a grave mischance is done, its card showeth **📝 Review after the mischance**. Read the course of events, then click **Make a card** beside each thing worth the changing.
9. Click **⋯ More**, then **🧩 Known follies**, to see problems that have a workaround. Click **🚀 Releases**, type a name such as v1.3 and click **🚀 A new release** to gather the done cards into notes. **↩ Undo** fileth a checklist card for undoing.
10. Click **⋯ More**, then **📆 Review** once a month: use **← Earlier** and **Later →** to change the month, and **✍️ Summary** for a summary of two lines from the on-call agent.
11. Click **⋯ More**, then **📈 Betterments** (also in the **❓ Help** menu) to see retro notions, review actions and mendings of trouble in one list. In **Setup**, click **Hold the review of access now** to see who may enter, then **Keep** or **Cast out** for each one.
guide.svc.full:
- **The service's particulars:** in **🎨 Look**, **The settings of the project**, **🛎️ Service** thou sayest what a project offereth, to whom, at what web address, and who is on call. Only projects thou tickest are counted services.
- **Uptime dot:** every few minutes the board asketh the web address if it liveth. Green is well; red signifieth it answered not. Three misses together open one incident, never a heap, and a remark telleth when it returned ("Up again after N min").
- **Reply by ⏰:** each kind of card hath a time of answer (an incident about an hour, a friend's request some two days, a bug about a week). Tardy cards turn red and the daily brief listeth them. These be aims, not vows.
- **🚨 Grave:** for an incident that grieveth many users or putteth coin or data in peril. One click raiseth the swarm, rouseth the on-call agent, sendeth thee one note, and asketh a "Status:" remark every 30 minutes.
- **Status page:** a public page showeth each public service as green, orange or red with the latest status line. It never showeth card text, only the line thou or the agent didst choose.
- **Service desk:** reports from friends and the feedback form are sorted into **Request**, **Incident** or **Notion**. The inbox filter (**Desk: all**, **Desk: requests** and the rest) showeth one kind. A report that resembleth a card thou hast already saith "looketh like AIG-12" with a **Link** button.
- **🧩 Known follies:** a problem whose cause is known and that hath a workaround, yet is not mended. They are listed per project and for all projects, and go into each agent's brief, that none search twice.
- **📖 Runbooks:** short notes, step by step, on how to mend a thing. An incident card showeth those that match its title. After a review, the agent may propose a new runbook and thou sayest Go or Not yet.
- **📝 Review after the mischance:** when a grave mischance is done, the agent writeth the **Course of events**, **What did help** and **What to mend**. Each action becometh a card with **Make a card**. If no agent be free, thou writest it thyself.
- **🗂️ Items:** the list of things a service standeth on, with a **Kind** (server, domain, certificate, key, repo, purveyor, other). Each may bear links to cards or web addresses. A key is but its name from Secrets, never the key itself. Incident and change cards may show what they **Affect**.
- **Expiry and backups:** each day the board examineth expiry dates and the age of backups. A card appeareth ere aught runneth out or when a backup groweth too old, and once a month a restore-test card remindeth thee that a backup never tried in restoring is but a hope.
- **Health of the server:** the board watcheth CPU, memory and disk upon thy servers and raiseth an upgrade card ere they fill.
- **🔐 Review of access:** every 90 days one card listeth share links, friends' roles and kept secrets (names only), each with **Keep** or **Cast out**. Hold it now from **Setup**.
- **🚀 Releases:** a release is a named bundle of the cards made done since the last, with short notes. **↩ Undo** fileth a checklist card with the steps for undoing.
- **📈 Betterments:** retro counsels, review actions and mendings of trouble in one list, to be sifted by project, that good notions be not lost between retros.
- **📆 Monthly review:** one page per service for one month: incidents opened and closed, the mean time to mend, cards that kept their time of answer, uptime, tokens spent and the server's peaks. Open it from **⋯ More → 📆 Review** or from **The settings of the project → Service**.
- **Monthly token cap:** in **The settings of the project → Service** thou mayst set a monthly bound of tokens. At 80% the daily brief doth warn thee; at 100% the background runs of that project wait till next month or till thou raise the cap. Thine own Rouse still worketh.
- **Good habits:** fill in the service's particulars first, keep the web address true, look upon the status dot daily, write up every grave mischance and peruse the betterments list after each retro, and read the monthly review whilst the month be fresh.
guide.svc.agents:
- Raise an incident: `aigile add <proj> "Site is down" --type incident`
- A problem's cause and workaround: `aigile problem <proj> AIG-9 --cause "..." --workaround "..."`
- Configuration items: `aigile ci <proj>` listeth them; `aigile ci <proj> add <kind> <name>` addeth one
- Runbooks: `aigile runbook <proj>` listeth them; `aigile runbook <proj> <name>` printeth one
- Grave mischance (owner or chief): `aigile major <proj> <incident id> --as NAME`; run it again to end it
- Review after the mischance: `aigile pir <proj> <incident id> --timeline ".." --helped ".." --actions "one | two" --as NAME`
- Runbook from a review: `aigile pir-runbook <proj> <incident id> <name> --text ".." --as NAME`
- Releases: `aigile release <proj>` listeth; `aigile release <proj> <name> --as NAME` maketh one; add `rollback` to undo it
guide.msg.hi:
- **💬 Missives**, atop the left rail, holdeth all thy chats: project chiefs, friends, companies of agents and each project's Council Chamber. The filters **🤖 Agents**, **🙋 People** and **🎥 Council Chambers** show one kind.
- A **DM** is a private chat with one chief or one friend. Chats with friends are ciphered upon the way and upon this computer.
- A **company** setteth two agents or more in one chat: write once and each of them answereth.
- In a friend's chat, **📞 Call** beginneth a call of voice or video, with **🖥️ Show screen**. Each project's Council Chamber hath its own **🎥 Join the call**.
- Mic or camera barred? Allow it in the browser's address bar. Thou mayst ever still listen.
guide.msg.steps:
1. Click **💬 Missives** atop the left rail. Pick a filter to see only **🤖 Agents**, **🙋 People** or **🎥 Council Chambers**.
2. Click a project's chief to speak with that team directly. Type and press Enter; the chief answereth in the same chat.
3. Click a friend under **🙋 People** to chat with them. A friend appeareth here once they have joined by thy invitation.
4. To ask several agents at once, click **＋ A new company**, give it a name, tick two agents or more and click **Forge**.
5. In a friend's chat click **📞 Call**. Thy friend seeth thou art calling and clicketh to join. Use **🔇 Hush**, **📷 Eye awake** and **🖥️ Show screen**, and **Depart the call** when thou art done.
6. Under **🎥 Council Chambers**, open a project's chamber to speak with its whole team in one chat. Click **🎥 Join the call** for its call of voice or video.
7. The first time, the browser asketh leave for the microphone: click **Allow**. Saidst thou no in error? Click the sign at the start of the address bar, allow the microphone and call again.
guide.msg.full:
- **One place for every chat:** **💬 Missives** listeth chiefs, friends, companies and Council Chambers together, the newest first. The filters change only what thou seest; naught is moved or deleted.
- **Chiefs:** every project hath a chief. Their chat is the swiftest way to ask that team aught without making a card. Each answer is an agent's run, and so it spendeth tokens.
- **Friends:** a friend keepeth their own AI-gile. Thy DMs pass between thy two boards, ciphered, and are kept ciphered upon this computer too. Replies, reactions and typing dots work as in any chat app.
- **Companies:** thou and two agents or more, from any project. Each missive thou writest rouseth each member once to reply, so a great company spendeth more tokens.
- **Council Chambers:** one to each project, with the agents of its team as members, ever up to date. The call in a Council Chamber is for thee alone: friends and agents may not join it.
- **Calls:** calls of voice and video work straightway through AI-gile's own call server, for thee and for thy friend; naught to set up. To use thine own LiveKit server, open **Setup → Calls → Advanced**.
- **Screen showing:** in a call click **🖥️ Show screen**; the browser asketh which screen, window or tab. Click **🖥️ Cease showing** to stop.
- **Microphone, camera and speaker:** the call panel hath a chooser for each, handy with a headset or a second camera.
- **When mic or camera will not work:** "blocked" signifieth the browser said nay: allow it in the address bar. "Not found" signifieth naught is plugged in or switched on. "In use by another app" signifieth another call app holdeth it: close that one. Thou mayst ever still listen.
- **A call that faileth:** thou seest "Reconnecting…" first. If it end, look to thine internet and call again.
- **Good habits:** use a company or a Council Chamber for a question to several agents rather than copying it, hush thyself when thou speakest not, and show one window rather than the whole screen.
